common_name: Black Velvet Petunia (Near-Black Deep Purple Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Velvet was one of the first petunias bred to reach a genuinely near-black flower color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Velvet bears deep, velvety, near-black flowers with a soft matte texture, a dramatic, moody color rare among bedding annuals that makes it a favorite for designers looking to add contrast or a Gothic touch to a mixed container or border. Its rich color reads best against pale or bright companions like white, chartreuse, or silver-leaved plants rather than getting lost among other dark hues. Deadhead regularly or shear back by half in midsummer if growth becomes leggy, which prompts fresh, bushier regrowth and renewed bloom through fall.

common_name: Prism Sunshine Petunia (Clear Yellow Grandiflora Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Prism Sunshine is an AAS-winning grandiflora petunia noted for unusually clear, weather-resistant yellow color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Prism Sunshine bears large, clear, buttery-yellow grandiflora blooms that hold their color and form better in rain and heat than most earlier yellow petunias, a trait that earned it All-America Selections recognition when introduced. Its bright, cheerful color works well in mixed plantings with purples and blues, providing strong contrast without the harshness of orange or red. Deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and shear back by half in midsummer if plants become leggy, which encourages fresh, bushy regrowth.

common_name: Fantasy Pink Morn Petunia (Compact Pink-and-White Milliflora Petunia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Fantasy Pink Morn is a compact milliflora-type petunia bred for tidy, uniform bedding and container use.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Fantasy Pink Morn belongs to the milliflora class of petunia, bred for smaller, more numerous flowers on compact, densely branched plants rather than the fewer, larger blooms of grandiflora types, opening soft pink petals with a white star at the center in great profusion. Its tidy, uniform habit makes it especially well suited to edging, window boxes, and mixed containers where a large-flowered petunia would look coarse. It requires little deadheading to stay tidy and floriferous through the summer, and responds well to a midsummer shearing if growth becomes sparse in peak heat.

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained soil in full sun; Imagination is an AAS-winning spreading verbena noted for finely cut, lacy foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; verbena is drought tolerant once established and struggles in heavy, wet soil. Imagination bears profuse clusters of violet-blue flowers over unusually fine, lacy, deeply cut foliage that gives the plant a softer, more textured look than the broader leaves of most bedding verbena. Its trailing, spreading habit fills in quickly to cover bare ground, spill over a wall, or trail from a container, and it won an All-America Selections award for its exceptional heat tolerance and long bloom season. It is largely self-cleaning and needs little deadheading, but shearing lightly in midsummer refreshes growth if plants become sparse in peak heat.

common_name: King Edward VII Sweet Pea (Crimson-Scarlet Grandiflora Sweet Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; King Edward VII, introduced in 1897, was one of the earliest Grandiflora-type sweet peas.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Introduced in 1897, King Edward VII bears rich crimson-scarlet flowers that were larger and more vivid than earlier sweet pea cultivars of its day, helping launch the Grandiflora class of larger-flowered sweet peas and remaining a strongly fragrant, historically significant heirloom still grown today. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Matucana is a bicolor heirloom sweet pea prized for exceptionally strong fragrance.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Matucana bears richly bicolor flowers, deep maroon-red standards paired with violet-purple wings, closely related to the historic Cupani sweet pea and sharing its exceptionally strong, sweet fragrance, since both retain much of the intense scent that was gradually bred out of larger, more refined modern hybrids. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.

Blue Ripple bears large, ruffled, Spencer-type flowers on a white ground flecked and striped with blue-violet, an unusual broken-color pattern that gives every bloom a distinctive, painterly look and makes for eye-catching cut arrangements. Noel Sutton bears large, ruffled, richly fragrant Spencer-type flowers in a true, clear mid-blue considered one of the finest blue sweet peas ever raised, long used as the benchmark against which other blue cultivars are judged by exhibitors and breeders. Regular picking for the vase encourages continued bloom, since sweet peas stop flowering once they begin setting seed pods. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before summer heat ends the season.
